trivia: I have a horseback contest in which riders race to seize a goat or calf carcass and carry it to a scoring area while rival teams try to wrest it away.

I have Kuchi pastoralists, a mobile social community rather than a single ethnic group, who traditionally move twice a year with sheep and goats between mountain foothills, plains and dry-season pastures.

I have a rural tradition called ashar: when a household needs help harvesting wheat, building a mud house or clearing an irrigation canal, neighbours turn up to work without wages, knowing the favour will be returned when their turn comes.

I have Pashtun communities whose customary code, Pashtunwali, places great weight on hospitality, granting refuge to someone who asks for protection, and settling disputes through councils known as jirgas.

I have a small Pashayi boys' fashion subculture in an eastern mountain village: its teenagers decorate their caps with butterflies, flowers and even incense, then add embroidered outfits, henna-painted nails and dark eye makeup.
I have Kyrgyz families in the high Pamir where a traditional colour code marks a change in a woman's life: unmarried girls wear red veils, while married women wear white.

I have saffron fields around Herat where women begin picking purple crocus flowers at dawn, then separate the tiny red stigmas by hand; a woman-led company reported employing more than 1,000 women pickers in 2021.

I have a women-run radio station that turned its airwaves into a classroom after girls were barred from secondary school; it broadcasts six hours of curriculum-based lessons each day, three in Dari and three in Pashto.

I have a folk protective charm called a tawiz: a religious scholar may write Qur'anic verses on a tiny slip of paper, fold it into a pouch and have it worn by a child for protection from illness or the evil eye.

I have a 35-article morality law issued by the Taliban's de facto authorities in August 2024; it requires women to cover their bodies and faces in public and restricts their use of public transport without a male guardian.

I have a Pashto folk-poetry form called a landay: an anonymous couplet passed from voice to voice, with 22 syllables arranged as nine in the first line and thirteen in the second; its subjects range from love and grief to war and homeland.
I have a communal circle dance called Attan, in which dancers move in a ring to drums that gradually quicken, making the steps and turns faster and more intense.

I share the rubab, a plucked string instrument traditionally made with a wooden body and a skin-covered soundboard; UNESCO recognised its crafting and playing as shared heritage across four countries in 2024.
I welcome the spring new year in Mazar-e-Sharif with Janda Bala, a ceremony in which a great banner is raised at a shrine; the surrounding hills are known for their spring display of red tulips.

I have a fine embroidery from Kandahar called khamak: girls may begin learning its precise geometric stitching from their mothers and grandmothers as young as five, and a single elaborate shawl can take months to complete.

I have a tile-making workshop inside Herat's Grand Mosque where artisans still use hand tools and techniques passed down for about 850 years; its tiles have been made with stone from the Hari Rud and lapis from Badakhshan.
I have a village whose pottery is famous for a sea-green glaze made by burning the root of a local ishkar plant, grinding its ash and mixing it with quartz and copper oxide before firing the pots.

I have a Nowruz ritual in some Wakhi homes in which people use flour-tipped wooden sticks to draw designs on the ceiling, leave the sticks there through the year and burn them when the next new year arrives.
I have remote Wakhan homes that set aside a mehmankhana, a room reserved for guests; travellers may be welcomed and fed there even when they arrive as complete strangers.
I once had street photographers who used the kamra-e-faoree, a handmade wooden box that served as both camera and darkroom, producing a black-and-white portrait in only a few minutes.
I mark the spring new year with Haft Mewa, a sweet compote made by soaking seven kinds of dried fruit and nuts overnight until they become a festive dish to share.
I have a stuffed flatbread called bolani that can be filled with pumpkin, potato or leeks; one savoury pumpkin version is seasoned with cumin, coriander and garlic, then folded and fried until crisp.
I have a celebratory dumpling called mantu: thin dough is folded around spiced meat and onion, steamed, then served under tomato sauce and a thick, strained-yogurt topping.
I have Pamir households that preserve sour milk as qurut: small, salted balls of dried curd that keep for long periods without refrigeration.
I have supplied deep-blue lapis lazuli from the Sar-i-Sang mines in Badakhshan since antiquity; the stone travelled across long trade routes to Mesopotamia by the third millennium BCE.
I have a centuries-old irrigation system called karez: gently sloping underground tunnels tap groundwater near the mountains and carry it by gravity to fields, reducing the water lost to the hot sun.

I have the Sarai Shahzada market in Kabul, a dense bazaar of currency exchangers and money brokers where the informal hawala network helps move payments between cities without transporting the same banknotes from one place to another.

I have a vast copper deposit at Mes Aynak that lies beneath an archaeological landscape of Buddhist monasteries, stupas and settlements; plans to mine the copper have therefore raised a difficult question about industry and heritage.

I piloted a mobile-money system to pay police salaries directly to their phones; in one trial, officers found they were taking home about a third more once intermediaries could no longer skim their wages.
I have Band-e-Amir, a chain of six deep-blue lakes separated by natural travertine dams that are slowly built as mineral-rich water deposits calcium carbonate.
I have a high-altitude lake at Dasht-e Nawar, about 3,200 metres above sea level, that has been described as the world's highest breeding ground for greater flamingos.
I have a high-mountain population of Marco Polo sheep, a wild sheep whose enormous curling horns can approach two metres from tip to tip.

I have a narrow eastern strip of land that reaches China's border while running between Tajikistan and Pakistan; this long, high-mountain corridor is one of the most remote inhabited regions in the Hindu Kush and Pamirs.
I gained recognition of my independence in foreign affairs through a 1919 treaty with Britain.
I saw carpet designs change after the Soviet invasion of 1979: some weavers began putting tanks, helicopters, guns and other weapons into patterns that had once been mainly geometric or floral.

I saw a British-Indian army retreat from Kabul in January 1842 with thousands of soldiers and camp followers; the only European to reach Jalalabad with the retreating column was military surgeon William Brydon.

I kept the Bactrian Gold safe through years of conflict: after more than 20,000 objects were excavated from six ancient tombs, museum staff secretly hid the treasure in a central-bank vault, and it was revealed intact in 2003.

I witnessed a Soviet special-forces assault on Kabul's Tajbeg Palace in December 1979; the operation killed the country's leader and installed a replacement in an attack that lasted roughly 43 minutes.

I had mountain communities whose pre-Islamic religion included wooden sacred figures and shrines; after a campaign of forced conversion in 1895–96, the region's name was changed to one meaning 'Land of Light'.

I once had two giant Buddha figures carved into the cliffs of the Bamiyan Valley, one 55 metres tall and the other 38; both were destroyed in 2001, but the caves and painted Buddhist sanctuaries around them remain.
I have a 65-metre brick minaret built in the 12th century in a remote river valley; its surface is covered in intricate geometric brickwork and a high band of turquoise-tile inscription.

I had a major Greek-founded city called Ai-Khanoum from the late fourth to the mid-second century BCE; excavations uncovered the remains of a theatre, gymnasium and other buildings of a Hellenistic urban centre.
